items.title: IMSI Receives Incorrect IP From Device Group
items.body:
I have created:

-  two subscribers
- two device groups with one subscriber each
- one slice with both device groups

On UE attach, both subscribers receive IP addresses from the same subnet range.

# Steps to Reproduce

## Provision Data

To make this easier to reproduce, I used `curl` directly against the `webconsole` container.

### Subscribers

```bash
for IMSI in `seq 81 82`; do 
  curl -v ${WEBUI_IP}:5000/api/subscriber/imsi-2089301000074${IMSI} \
  --header 'Content-Type: text/plain' \
  --data "{
    \"UeId\":\"2089301000074${IMSI}\",
    \"opc\":\"981d464c7c52eb6e5036234984ad0bcf\",
    \"key\":\"5122250214c33e723a5dd523fc145fc0\",
    \"sequenceNumber\":\"16f3b3f70fc2\"
  }"
done
```

### Device Groups

```bash
curl -v ${WEBUI_IP}:5000/config/v1/device-group/DG-1 \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data '{
    "imsis": [
        "208930100007481"
    ],
    "site-info": "site-1",
    "ip-domain-name": "domain1",
    "ip-domain-expanded": {
        "dnn": "internet",
        "ue-ip-pool": "172.1.0.0/16",
        "dns-primary": "8.8.8.8",
        "mtu": 1348,
        "ue-dnn-qos": {
            "dnn-mbr-uplink":   10,
            "dnn-mbr-downlink": 10,
            "bitrate-unit": "mbps",
            "traffic-class": {
                "name": "platinum",
                "arp": 6,
                "pdb": 300,
                "pelr": 6,
                "qci": 8
            }
        }
    }
}'
```

```bash
curl -v ${WEBUI_IP}:5000/config/v1/device-group/DG-2 \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data '{
    "imsis": [
        "208930100007482"
    ],
    "site-info": "site-2",
    "ip-domain-name": "domain2",
    "ip-domain-expanded": {
        "dnn": "internet",
        "ue-ip-pool": "172.2.0.0/16",
        "dns-primary": "8.8.8.8",
        "mtu": 1348,
        "ue-dnn-qos": {
            "dnn-mbr-uplink":   20,
            "dnn-mbr-downlink": 20,
            "bitrate-unit": "mbps",
            "traffic-class": {
                "name": "platinum",
                "arp": 6,
                "pdb": 300,
                "pelr": 6,
                "qci": 8
            }
        }
    }
}'
```

### Slices

```bash
curl -v ${WEBUI_IP}:5000/config/v1/network-slice/Slice-1 \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data '
{
  "SliceName": "Slice-1",
  "slice-id": {
    "sst": "1",
    "sd": "010203"
  },
  "site-device-group": [
    "DG-2",
    "DG-1"
  ],
  "site-info": {
    "site-name": "demo",
    "plmn": {
      "mcc": "208",
      "mnc": "93"
    },
    "gNodeBs": [
      {
        "name": "gnbsim-gnbsim-gnbsim",
        "tac": 1
      }
    ],
    "upf": {
      "upf-name": "upf.mgmt",
      "upf-port": "8805"
    }
  }
}'
```

## Connect a UE

Using UERANSIM, I connected the gNB simulator, then proceeded to connect subscriber 1. The following was observed in the SMF log

```
2024-02-28T20:41:51.466Z [smf] 2024-02-28T20:41:51Z [INFO][SMF][PduSess][imsi-208930100007481][1][urn:uuid:a5da504c-e8a7-49a1-b096-d1392de9c811] PDUSessionSMContextCreate, IP alloc success IP[172.2.0.1]
```
IP allocation on the UESIM confirms receipt of this address:
```
[2024-02-28 20:41:51.556] [app] [info] Connection setup for PDU session[1] is successful, TUN interface[uesimtun0, 172.2.0.1] is up.
```

## Attachments

SCTP pcaps for the two IMSIs showing the setup, confirming that other values such as the AMBR do correspond to the correct device groups.

items.title: Proposal: Add SMF NAS supervision timers (T3591/T3592) and pending session states for reliability & NTN support
items.body:
Hi maintainers,

While testing SD-Core SMF for long-RTT scenarios (e.g., 5G NTN), we’ve identified that SMF currently does not implement NAS supervision timers such as T3591 (Session Modification) and T3592 (Session Release). Because of this, the SMF cannot retransmit NAS commands or detect NAS delivery failures, which can leave session procedures stuck.

To support NTN  and to improve reliability in terrestrial deployments I have the following proposal:
* new SMF session states (e.g., ModificationPending, ReleasePending)
* handling of NAS PDU Session Modification/Release  and associated Command/Complete
* supervision timers (T3591/T3592)
* retransmission logic

Before preparing a design or PR, I’d like to check in with maintainers to confirm:
- Whether this direction fits the roadmap
- Whether the preferred workflow is a single consolidated design issue or incremental PRs
- Whether adding new SMF states is acceptable in principle

Happy to provide a detailed design / state machine diagram after initial feedback. I am new to contributing to SD-Core SMF, so I'm happy to follow any preferred  guidelines for proposing and structuring changes. 
Thanks!

items.title: Bug: PDU Session Establishment fails after AMF pod restart due to stale CommunicationClient
items.body:
Hi maintainers,

While testing SD-Core in a Kubernetes deployment, we hit a reproducible failure where PDU Session Establishment stops working for all UEs after the AMF pod restarts. The UE registers fine, but never receives the PDU Session Establishment Accept — the T3580 timer expires and the UE retransmits indefinitely. Restarting the SMF pod is currently the only way to recover.

I’ve traced the root cause and would like to upstream a fix. Before opening the PR, I want to make sure the analysis and approach align with how you’d like to see this addressed.

## Symptom

```
[nas] Initial Registration is successful
[nas] Sending PDU Session Establishment Request
[nas] Retransmitting PDU Session Establishment Request due to T3580 expiry
[nas] Retransmitting PDU Session Establishment Request due to T3580 expiry
... up to 5 times → PDU Session Establishment procedure failure
```

SMF logs show the N1N2MessageTransfer hanging:

```
producer/pdu_session.go: send N1N2Transfer failed,
  Post "https://10.x.y.OLD:29518/namf-comm/v1/.../n1-n2-messages":
  dial tcp 10.x.y.OLD:29518: i/o timeout
```

…where `10.x.y.OLD` is the AMF pod IP from before the restart.

## Why registration works but PDU session fails

Registration uses NGAP/SCTP via the K8s Service for the AMF, which transparently routes to the current pod. PDU session establishment adds an HTTP return path (SMF → AMF `N1N2MessageTransfer`) that uses the AMF’s **pod IP** from the NRF profile, baked into a per-SMContext `CommunicationClient` at session creation time. When the AMF pod restarts with a new IP, the NGAP path keeps working but the cached HTTP endpoint is dead.

| Step | Addressing | Survives AMF pod restart? |
|------|-----------|--------------------------|
| gNB → AMF (registration) | K8s Service IP : 38412 | Yes |
| AMF → SMF (CreateSMContext) | Fresh NRF lookup at call time | Yes |
| **SMF → AMF (N1N2MessageTransfer)** | **Cached AMF pod IP in SMContext.CommunicationClient** | **No** |

## Root cause (4 interacting layers)

1. **`SMContext.CommunicationClient` is built once and never refreshed.**
   In `producer/pdu_session.go::PDUSessionSMContextCreate`, the SMF discovers the AMF via NRF and constructs `Namf_Communication.NewAPIClient(...)` with `SetBasePath(service.ApiPrefix)`. The client lives on the SMContext and is reused for every subsequent N1N2MessageTransfer (in `producer/pdu_session.go`, `producer/callback.go`, `pfcp/handler/handler.go`, `pfcp/message/send.go`). It is also tagged `json:"communicationClient,omitempty"`, so after SMF restart and DB recovery it is `nil`.

2. **NRF accumulates stale NF profiles.** Every AMF/SMF pod restart creates a new registration; old ones are never cleaned up (no preStop deregistration, no heartbeat-based TTL). The NRF can end up with multiple AMF entries pointing to dead pod IPs. (Filed separately for the NRF — happy to link if useful.)

3. **NRF cache returns stale entries on re-discovery.** SMF’s NRF cache (`nrfCacheEvictionInterval` default 900s, per-entry 1-minute TTL) caches the first AMF profile it sees. A targeted lookup by old `ServingNfId` keeps returning the same dead entry. So even calling `SendNFDiscoveryServingAMF` again does not refresh the endpoint.

4. **No HTTP timeout on the openapi client.** `Namf_Communication.APIClient` uses `http.DefaultClient`, no timeout. A TCP connect to a dead pod IP hangs ~60s waiting for kernel timeout — far longer than the UE’s T3580 (~16s), so any application-level retry is moot because the call hasn’t returned yet.

## When this is observed in the field

The most common report is the “overnight UE” pattern: a UE registers in the evening, the AMF pod is silently rolled at 2 a.m. (Helm upgrade, OOM, node drain, liveness probe), and in the morning re-registration succeeds but every PDU session attempt fails with T3580 expiry. The bug requires the AMF endpoint to change at some point — but in any K8s environment this happens routinely and invisibly.

In multi-pod clusters the failure can persist indefinitely because per-SMContext `CommunicationClient` instances are independent — even if the NRF cache is later refreshed by a new session creation, existing SMContexts retain their stale clients.

## Proposed fix (defensive, SMF-side)

Add a retry wrapper that all N1N2MessageTransfer call sites use:

1. **Short HTTP timeout (5s) on each attempt** via `context.WithTimeout` so we fail fast and stay well inside the T3580 window.
2. **On failure, query NRF directly bypassing the cache** (using the existing `SendNrfForNfInstance` codepath) and iterate through every returned AMF candidate with a different `NfInstanceId` than the one that just failed. This handles the multi-stale-entry case where NRF has more than one dead registration.
3. **Reconstruct `CommunicationClient` from the stored `AMFProfile` after DB recovery** (new `SMContext.RebuildCommunicationClient()` method called from `context/db.go`) so post-SMF-restart sessions have a usable client.

The four direct `CommunicationClient.N1N2MessageTransfer` call sites become single-line calls to the wrapper. Total change is ~134 lines added, ~23 removed across 7 files (`consumer/nf_management.go`, `context/sm_context.go`, `context/db.go`, `producer/pdu_session.go`, `producer/callback.go`, `pfcp/handler/handler.go`, `pfcp/message/send.go`).

Happy path is unchanged: cached client succeeds, no extra NRF roundtrip, no retry. Recovery path: 5s timeout → NRF direct query → iterate candidates → first live AMF wins. In our testing on RKE2 + UERANSIM, end-to-end recovery after AMF kill is ~5–11s vs. permanent failure without the fix.

## Verification

We A/B tested stock `rel-3.1.0` against the patched build on two RKE2 clusters:

| Metric | Stock `rel-3.1.0` SMF | Patched SMF |
|--------|----------------------|-------------|
| Baseline PDU session | success | success |
| After `kubectl delete pod -l app=amf` (new pod IP) | T3580 expires 5×, procedure failure | Accept on first or second attempt, ~5–11s |
| Recovery on multiple stale NRF entries | permanent failure | iterates through dead entries, succeeds on live AMF |

## Question for maintainers

Before I open the PR I’d like to check:

- Does the framing (defensive retry + cache-bypass re-discovery + DB-recovery rebuild) make sense to you, or would you prefer a different approach (e.g. removing the per-SMContext `CommunicationClient` entirely and looking up via the NRF cache on every call)?
- Are you happy with the change being a single commit, or would you prefer it split (e.g. `RebuildCommunicationClient` + DB recovery as one PR, retry/timeout/re-discovery as a follow-up)?
- Any preference on whether unit tests should accompany this fix, or is it acceptable to ship without (similar to recent fix-style PRs)?

Happy to provide a more detailed sequence diagram or full A/B test logs if useful. Branch is ready locally and signed off.

Thanks!
